title: Land Law
topics: Estates, interests and the nature of land

notes.h: Land, estates and interests: the 1925 framework
notes.body:
Land law sets out which rights in land exist, how they are created and who they bind. "Land" is defined broadly in the Law of Property Act 1925 s205(1)(ix): it includes buildings, parts of buildings and incorporeal rights such as easements. Ownership runs above and below the surface, but only to the height needed for ordinary use (Bernstein v Skyviews (1978)).

Fixtures and chattels. A fixture becomes part of the land and passes on sale; a chattel does not. Holland v Hodgson (1872) asks about the degree of annexation and, more importantly, the object of annexation. Elitestone v Morris [1997] held that a bungalow resting on concrete pillars, which could only be removed by demolishing it, was part of the land. In Botham v TSB Bank [1996], carpets, curtains and freestanding white goods remained chattels.

Estates and interests. The LPA 1925 s1(1) cut legal estates down to two: the fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold). Section 1(2) lists the interests that can be legal: easements equivalent to a legal estate, rentcharges, charges by way of legal mortgage and rights of entry. Under s1(3) every other right is equitable only, for example a life interest, a restrictive covenant or a beneficial interest under a trust.

Formalities.
- A legal estate or interest has to be created by deed: LPA 1925 s52, with the requirements for a valid deed in the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 s1. Leases of up to three years are excepted by s54(2).
- A contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, contain all the agreed terms and be signed by both parties: LP(MP)A 1989 s2.
- A legal disposition that is not made by deed may still take effect in equity if it counts as a specifically enforceable contract (Walsh v Lonsdale (1882)).

Illustration. A grants B a right of way for 10 years in a signed letter, not a deed. The right cannot be legal. If the letter meets s2, B has an equitable easement. In registered land it needs protection by a notice to bind a purchaser.

Exam pitfalls.
- Classify a right as legal or equitable before moving on to who it binds. The answer decides which priority rules apply.
- Do not treat s2 as a rule about deeds. It governs contracts, and a contract that fails s2 is void, not merely unenforceable.
- Remember that whether something is a fixture depends on its purpose, not just on how firmly it is attached.

notes.h: Registered land under the Land Registration Act 2002
notes.body:
The LRA 2002 aims to make the register a complete and accurate record of title, so a buyer need not investigate the title's history.

First registration. Under s4, a transfer of an unregistered freehold, a grant of a lease of more than seven years, or a first legal mortgage makes registration compulsory. Under ss6–7 the application must be made within two months, or the legal title reverts to the transferor, who then holds it on bare trust.

Registrable dispositions. Under s27, transfers, leases of more than seven years, express legal easements and legal charges operate at law only once registered. Until then the grantee holds only an equitable interest.

Priority. Section 28 sets the basic rule: priority follows the order of creation. Section 29 creates the key exception. A registrable disposition made for valuable consideration and completed by registration takes free of any earlier interest unless that interest is:
- protected by a notice on the register (s32), or
- overriding under Schedule 3. A restriction (s40) gives no priority. It limits how dispositions can be made, for example by requiring payment to two trustees.

Schedule 3 overriding interests.
- Para 1: legal leases of seven years or less.
- Para 2: the interests of people in actual occupation. An interest does not override if the occupier failed to disclose it when reasonably asked. It also does not override if the occupation would not have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection and the buyer did not actually know of the interest.
- Para 3: unregistered legal easements and profits, subject to conditions on knowledge, obviousness and use.

Key cases. Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland [1981]: a wife in actual occupation, with a beneficial interest, bound the bank. Abbey National v Cann [1991]: occupation is tested at completion, and the interest itself must exist at the date of registration. Link Lending v Bustard [2010]: an occupier detained in a psychiatric unit was still in actual occupation. City of London BS v Flegg [1988]: payment to two trustees overreaches the beneficial interests, so actual occupation does not help the beneficiaries.

Alteration and indemnity. Schedule 4 allows the register to be altered, including rectification where a mistake is corrected and the correction prejudices the registered proprietor. Schedule 8 compensates people who suffer loss through rectification or a mistake. The register is conclusive under s58, but registering a forged disposition is a mistake that can be corrected, with indemnity paid to whoever loses out (Swift 1st v Chief Land Registrar [2015]).

Exam pitfalls.
- Check value was given: a donee is bound by everything (s28).
- Occupation alone is not enough. The occupier must also have a proprietary interest.

When two or more people own land together, the legal title is always held on a trust of land: LPA 1925 ss34–36 and the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 (TOLATA). The legal title must be held as a joint tenancy by no more than four trustees (Trustee Act 1925 s34). In equity, the beneficial interests may be held either as a joint tenancy or as a tenancy in common.

Joint tenancy and tenancy in common.
- Joint tenants together own the whole. The right of survivorship applies, and joint tenancy needs the four unities of possession, interest, title and time (AG Securities v Vaughan [1990]).
- Tenants in common have separate, undivided shares that can pass by will. Only unity of possession is needed.
- Words of severance such as "equally" or "in equal shares" create a tenancy in common. Equity presumes a tenancy in common for business partners, unequal contributions and joint mortgagees (Malayan Credit v Jack Chia-MPH [1986]). For a domestic home bought in joint names, Stack v Dowden [2007] instead starts from a beneficial joint tenancy, even where contributions were unequal. An express declaration is conclusive in the absence of fraud or mistake (Goodman v Gallant [1986]).

Severance of a beneficial joint tenancy.
- Written notice under LPA s36(2). It takes effect when it is delivered to the other joint tenant's address, even if never read (Kinch v Bullard [1999]). It must show an intention to sever immediately (Harris v Goddard [1983]).
- The three methods in Williams v Hensman (1861): an act operating on one's own share, such as a sale or a mortgage; mutual agreement; and a course of dealing (Burgess v Rawnsley [1975]).
- Unlawful killing severs under the forfeiture rule. Severance never applies to the legal title.

TOLATA disputes. Sections 12–13 give beneficiaries rights of occupation. Under s14 any trustee or person with an interest can apply to court, which considers the factors in s15: the settlors' intentions, the purposes of the trust, the welfare of any minor in occupation, and the interests of secured creditors. Mortgage Corp v Shaire [2001] confirmed that s15 widened the court's discretion, but creditors usually obtain sale (Bank of Ireland v Bell [2001]). Where a beneficiary is bankrupt, Insolvency Act 1986 s335A applies. After one year the creditors' interests prevail unless the circumstances are exceptional (Re Citro [1991]; Barca v Mears [2004]).

Illustration. A, B and C buy as beneficial joint tenants. A sells her share to D, which severs it. B then dies. In equity C now holds two-thirds and D one-third as tenants in common. A's sale of her beneficial share does not affect the legal title, so A and C hold the legal title as trustees for C and D.

Exam pitfalls.
- Keep the legal title and the beneficial interests separate in every answer.
- Overreaching (LPA ss2 and 27) needs payment to at least two trustees or a trust corporation.

A lease is a term of years absolute (LPA 1925 s1(1)(b)). A licence is a personal permission that does not bind successors.

Lease or licence. Street v Mountford [1985] held that exclusive possession for a term, usually at a rent, creates a tenancy, whatever label the parties use. Exceptions include no intention to create legal relations, service occupiers and lodgers. Sham terms are disregarded: in Antoniades v Villiers [1990] a clause allowing the landlord to move others into a small flat was ignored. In AG Securities v Vaughan [1990], separate agreements created licences because the unities were missing.

Certainty of term. The maximum duration must be certain from the outset (Lace v Chantler [1944]; Prudential Assurance v London Residuary Body [1992]). In Mexfield Housing Co-op v Berrisford [2011] the Supreme Court held that an uncertain term granted to an individual took effect at common law as a lease for life. LPA s149(6) then converted it into a 90-year term, determinable on death. Periodic tenancies are valid because each period is certain.

Formalities. A legal lease needs a deed (s52), except a lease of up to three years that takes effect in possession, is at the best rent and is granted without a fine (s54(2)). Leases of more than seven years must be registered (LRA 2002 s27(2)(b)). An informal lease may be equitable under Walsh v Lonsdale (1882). Bruton v London & Quadrant [2000] recognised a contractual, non-proprietary "lease" that binds the parties only.

Covenants. For leases granted on or after 1 January 1996, the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 passes the benefit and burden of all covenants with the reversion and the term (s3). Under s5 the tenant is released on a lawful assignment, although they may be required to give an authorised guarantee agreement (s16). For older leases, covenants that "touch and concern" the land run with the lease and reversion (Spencer's Case (1583); P&A Swift Investments v Combined English Stores [1989]), and the original tenant remains liable on privity of contract.

Remedies. Forfeiture requires a re-entry clause. For breaches other than non-payment of rent, an LPA s146 notice must first be served, and the tenant can seek relief. Accepting rent knowing of the breach waives forfeiture. Residential occupiers can only be evicted through court proceedings (Protection from Eviction Act 1977 ss2–3). The Renters' Rights Act 2025 abolishes assured shorthold tenancies and "no-fault" section 21 possession for private residential tenancies in England. Its main tenancy reforms came into force on 1 May 2026, when existing assured shorthold tenancies became periodic assured tenancies and landlords must rely on a statutory possession ground.

Exam pitfalls.
- Do not stop at the label in the document. Apply Street v Mountford and look for a sham.
- Check when the lease was granted before choosing the rules on covenants.

An easement is a right over one piece of land (the servient tenement) for the benefit of another (the dominant tenement), such as a right of way, light or drainage.

Essential characteristics (Re Ellenborough Park [1956]).
- There must be a dominant and a servient tenement.
- The right must accommodate the dominant tenement. It has to benefit the land itself, not just the current owner personally (Hill v Tupper (1863)).
- The two tenements must be owned or occupied by different people.
- The right must be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant. It must be definite, of a recognised kind, and not amount to exclusive possession (Copeland v Greenhalf [1952]; Batchelor v Marlow [2003]). Moncrieff v Jamieson [2007] suggests the test is whether the servient owner keeps reasonable use of the land. Regency Villas v Diamond Resorts [2018] accepted that recreational and sporting rights can be easements.

Acquisition.
- Express grant or reservation by deed. In registered land, an express legal easement must be registered (LRA 2002 s27(2)(d)).
- Implied by necessity, where the land would otherwise be unusable.
- Implied by common intention, where the easement is needed to give effect to the parties' shared purpose (Pwllbach Colliery v Woodman [1915]).
- Wheeldon v Burrows (1879). On a grant of part of land, quasi-easements pass if they were continuous and apparent, necessary for reasonable enjoyment, and in use at the time of the grant. The rule applies only to grants, not to reservations.
- LPA 1925 s62. A conveyance converts existing rights and advantages, including licences, into easements (Wright v Macadam [1949]). Diversity of occupation is normally required (Long v Gowlett [1923]), but not where the right was continuous and apparent (Platt v Crouch [2003]; Wood v Waddington [2015]).
- Prescription. Use as of right (without force, secrecy or permission) for 20 years, at common law, by lost modern grant or under the Prescription Act 1832.

Priority. Legal easements that arise by implication or prescription override a registered disposition under Sch 3 para 3, but only if the buyer knew of them, they would have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, or they were exercised in the year before the disposition. Equitable easements need a notice.

Illustration. V sells the front of her plot to P, keeping the rear, which is reached by a track over the front. Any right for V is a reservation, so she must show necessity or common intention.

Exam pitfalls.
- Do not apply Wheeldon v Burrows to reservations.
- Rights that amount to exclusive use, such as the storage in Copeland, fail the "capable of grant" requirement.

A freehold covenant is a promise by deed by one landowner (the covenantor) for the benefit of another's land (the covenantee). The question is whether it binds and benefits successors.

Burden.
- At common law the burden of a covenant never runs with freehold land (Austerberry v Oldham Corp (1885)). Rhone v Stephens [1994] confirmed this for a positive covenant to repair a roof.
- In equity the burden of a restrictive covenant can run under Tulk v Moxhay (1848). Four conditions apply: (1) the covenant must be negative in substance; (2) the covenantee must have retained land that the covenant benefits (London County Council v Allen [1914]); (3) the parties must have intended the burden to run, which is presumed under LPA s79; and (4) the successor must be bound under the priority rules. In registered land that means protection by notice. In unregistered land it means a Class D(ii) land charge for covenants made after 1925.
- Substance, not wording, decides: "not to let the fence fall into disrepair" is positive.

Benefit.
- At common law the benefit passes if the covenant touches and concerns the land, the original covenantee had a legal estate, the successor holds a legal estate, and the parties intended it to run. LPA s78 can supply that intention (Smith and Snipes Hall Farm v River Douglas Catchment Board [1949]).
- In equity the benefit passes by one of three routes. Annexation can be express, implied or statutory (Federated Homes v Mill Lodge [1980]); s78 annexes the benefit to land that can be identified (Crest Nicholson v McAllister [2004]), unless it is excluded. Assignment must be made together with the land. A scheme of development applies where the conditions in Elliston v Reacher [1908] are met.
- If the burden passes in equity, the benefit must pass in equity too.

Getting positive obligations to bind successors.
- A chain of indemnity covenants.
- The benefit and burden principle (Halsall v Brizell [1957]). The burden must be relevant to the benefit being taken, and the successor must have a real choice whether to take the benefit (Thamesmead Town v Allotey (1998)).
- A long lease, estate rentcharge or commonhold.
- The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 can pass the benefit to identifiable future owners.

Discharge or modification. The Upper Tribunal can discharge or modify a covenant under LPA s84, for example where it is obsolete or impedes reasonable use. Alexander Devine Children's Cancer Trust v Housing Solutions [2020] held that a developer's deliberate breach can count heavily against it.

Exam pitfalls.
- Always deal with burden and benefit separately, at law and in equity.
- Positive burdens never run, however drafted.

A mortgage is security for a debt. In registered land a legal mortgage can only be created as a charge by deed expressed to be by way of legal mortgage (LRA 2002 s23; LPA ss85–87). It takes effect at law only once it is registered (s27(2)(f)). Priority between registered charges follows the order on the register (s48).

The equity of redemption. The borrower keeps the right to redeem, and equity protects that right.
- There must be no clog or fetter on redemption. A lender's option to buy the property, granted as part of the mortgage, is void (Samuel v Jarrah Timber [1904]). An option granted in a separate, later transaction may survive.
- Collateral advantages are valid unless unfair or unconscionable or clogging redemption (Kreglinger v New Patagonia Meat [1914]; contrast Noakes v Rice [1902]).
- Postponing redemption is acceptable in a commercial bargain between parties of equal strength (Knightsbridge Estates v Byrne [1939]).
- Oppressive terms can be struck down (Cityland v Dabrah [1968]), but a hard bargain stands (Multiservice Bookbinding v Marden [1979]). Most residential mortgages are also regulated under FSMA 2000 and the FCA's MCOB rules.

Undue influence. Where a wife or other person stands surety for another's debts, the lender is put on inquiry whenever the relationship is non-commercial. Under Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001] the lender is protected if it takes reasonable steps, usually by obtaining confirmation that the surety received independent legal advice.

Lender's remedies.
- Possession. The lender may take possession at any time, even without default (Four-Maids v Dudley Marshall [1957]). Peaceable entry without a court order is lawful in principle (Ropaigealach v Barclays [2000]), but court proceedings are normal. Under the Administration of Justice Act 1970 s36 (and AJA 1973 s8) the court can adjourn or suspend possession of a dwelling where the borrower is likely to pay off the arrears within a reasonable period, which can be the remaining term (Cheltenham & Gloucester BS v Norgan [1996]).
- Sale. The power arises under LPA s101 and becomes exercisable under s103. The lender must take reasonable care to obtain the true market value on the day it chooses to sell (Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance [1971]), but it may choose its own timing (Silven Properties v RBS [2003]). Surplus proceeds are held on trust under s105. Under s91 the court can order a sale at the borrower's request (Palk v Mortgage Services Funding [1993]).
- Appointing a receiver (s109), suing on the personal covenant, or (rarely) foreclosure.

Exam pitfalls.
- Separate the remedies, and check whether s36 applies (a dwelling).
- Etridge steps matter only if undue influence or misrepresentation actually occurred.

Adverse possession. A squatter can acquire title by possessing land without consent.

What possession requires (Powell v McFarlane (1977); JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2002]):
- factual possession: an appropriate degree of physical control for that type of land, such as enclosure or exclusive use; and
- an intention to possess: an intention to exclude everyone, including the paper owner, so far as is reasonably practicable. An intention to own is not needed, and willingness to pay if asked does not defeat the claim. Possession under a licence or with permission is not adverse.

Unregistered land. Under the Limitation Act 1980 s15 the owner's right to recover is barred after 12 years, and s17 extinguishes their title.

Registered land: LRA 2002 Sch 6.
- After 10 years' adverse possession the squatter can apply to be registered. The owner is notified and may serve a counter-notice.
- If a counter-notice is served, the application fails unless one of the para 5 conditions is met: (a) estoppel; (b) some other right to the land; or (c) a boundary case, where the squatter reasonably believed for 10 years that the land was theirs (Zarb v Parry [2011]; IAM Group v Chowdrey [2012]).
- If the owner then fails to evict the squatter within two years, the squatter may reapply and must be registered (para 6).
- Criminal squatting in a residential building (LASPO 2012 s144) still counts (Best v Chief Land Registrar [2015]). Pye v UK (2007) found no breach of Article 1 of Protocol 1.

Proprietary estoppel. Equity intervenes where a person relies to their detriment on an assurance of a right in land.
- Assurance. It must be clear enough in context and need not be express (Thorner v Major [2009]). In commercial dealings "subject to contract" negotiations rarely meet this test (Cobbe v Yeoman's Row [2008]).
- Reliance and detriment, judged across the whole relationship (Gillett v Holt [2001]).
- Unconscionability in going back on the assurance.
- Remedy. The court satisfies the equity. Guest v Guest [2022] starts from fulfilling the expectation, then adjusts it, for example for early receipt, with proportionality still relevant (Jennings v Rice [2002]). An equity by estoppel binds successors from the moment it arises (LRA 2002 s116) and can override if the claimant is in actual occupation.

Illustration. A farmer repeatedly tells his nephew "the farm will be yours", and the nephew works for decades on low wages. Thorner suggests estoppel succeeds.

Exam pitfalls.
- Apply Sch 6, not the 12-year rule, to registered land, unless 12 years had already been completed before 13 October 2003.
- Do not merge the estoppel elements. Deal with each one in turn.

cards.f: What are the only two legal estates under LPA 1925 s1(1)?
cards.b: The fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold).

cards.f: Which interests can be legal under LPA 1925 s1(2)?
cards.b: Easements and profits equivalent to a legal estate, rentcharges, charges by way of legal mortgage, and rights of entry attached to a legal lease or rentcharge. Under s1(3) every other interest is equitable.

cards.f: What does LP(MP)A 1989 s2 require?
cards.b: A contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, contain all the expressly agreed terms, and be signed by or for each party. If it does not, there is no contract at all.

cards.f: What is the rule in Walsh v Lonsdale (1882)?
cards.b: A specifically enforceable contract to grant a legal interest creates an equivalent interest in equity, because equity treats as done what ought to be done.

cards.f: What test for fixtures did Holland v Hodgson (1872) set?
cards.b: The court looks first at the degree of annexation and then, more decisively, at the object of annexation: whether the item was attached to improve the land permanently or so it could be enjoyed better as a chattel.

cards.f: Why did the bungalow in Elitestone v Morris [1997] count as part of the land?
cards.b: It rested on pillars and could not be removed without being destroyed. That showed it was intended to be part of the realty, even though it was not fixed down.

cards.f: What did Bernstein v Skyviews (1978) decide about airspace?
cards.b: The owner's rights in the airspace only extend to the height needed for ordinary use and enjoyment of the land. Flying a plane high above to take photographs was not trespass.

cards.f: Which leases can be legal without a deed?
cards.b: Under LPA s54(2), leases of no more than three years that take effect in possession, are at the best rent reasonably obtainable and are granted without a fine.

cards.f: Which formality rule covers dispositions of an existing equitable interest?
cards.b: LPA 1925 s53(1)(c): they must be in writing and signed by the person disposing of the interest, or by an agent authorised in writing.

cards.f: What is the effect of LRA 2002 s29?
cards.b: A registrable disposition made for valuable consideration and completed by registration takes priority over earlier interests unless they are protected by a notice or are overriding under Sch 3.

cards.f: Name the three main overriding interests in LRA 2002 Sch 3.
cards.b: Para 1: legal leases of seven years or less. Para 2: interests of persons in actual occupation. Para 3: certain legal easements and profits.

cards.f: When will the interest of a person in actual occupation not override under Sch 3 para 2?
cards.b: Where the occupier failed to disclose it when asked and disclosure could reasonably have been expected. Also where the occupation was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection and the purchaser did not actually know of the interest.

cards.f: What did Abbey National v Cann [1991] decide about timing?
cards.b: Actual occupation must exist at the date of the disposition (completion), and the interest must exist at the date of registration. Preparatory acts such as carpet-laying before completion were not occupation.

cards.f: Why could Ms Bustard be in actual occupation in Link Lending v Bustard [2010]?
cards.b: Her absence in a psychiatric unit was involuntary, she intended to return, her belongings stayed at the house and she made regular visits.

cards.f: What is the difference between a notice and a restriction?
cards.b: A notice records a third-party interest and protects its priority (s32). A restriction controls how a disposition must be made, for example by requiring two trustees to receive the money, but gives no priority (s40).

cards.f: Which events trigger compulsory first registration?
cards.b: Under LRA 2002 s4: transfers of a qualifying freehold or of a lease with more than seven years left, grants of leases of more than seven years, and first legal mortgages of a qualifying estate.

cards.f: Why did the wife's interest fail in City of London BS v Flegg [1988]?
cards.b: The mortgage money was paid to two trustees, so the beneficial interests were overreached into the proceeds. Actual occupation cannot revive an interest that has been overreached.

cards.f: Does a donee of registered land take free of unprotected interests?
cards.b: No. Section 29 protects only dispositions made for valuable consideration. A donee takes subject to every earlier interest under the basic rule in s28.

cards.f: What is rectification under LRA 2002 Sch 4?
cards.b: An alteration of the register that corrects a mistake and prejudicially affects the registered proprietor's title. A person who suffers loss may be indemnified under Sch 8.

cards.f: What are the four unities?
cards.b: Possession, interest, title and time. All four are needed for a joint tenancy. A tenancy in common needs only unity of possession.

cards.f: What is the right of survivorship?
cards.b: When a joint tenant dies, their interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenants and not under their will or intestacy.

cards.f: In what three situations does equity presume a tenancy in common?
cards.b: Where purchase money was contributed unequally, where the purchasers are business partners, and where the co-owners lend money on mortgage (see Malayan Credit v Jack Chia [1986]). For a domestic home in joint names, Stack v Dowden [2007] starts instead from a beneficial joint tenancy.

cards.f: What did Kinch v Bullard [1999] decide?
cards.b: A notice of severance under LPA s36(2) is effective once it is delivered to the addressee's last known address, even if they never read it and the sender later regrets sending it.

cards.f: List the three Williams v Hensman (1861) methods of severance.
cards.b: An act operating on one's own share, such as a sale or mortgage; mutual agreement; and a mutual course of dealing showing the interests are to be treated as shares held in common.

cards.f: Why did severance happen in Burgess v Rawnsley [1975]?
cards.b: The parties had orally agreed that one would buy the other's share. Even though the deal later fell through, the Court of Appeal held that the agreement severed the joint tenancy.

cards.f: What factors must the court consider under TOLATA s15?
cards.b: The intentions of the people who created the trust, the purposes for which the property is held, the welfare of any minor who occupies or might reasonably be expected to occupy it, and the interests of secured creditors.

cards.f: What test applies to a sale application by a trustee in bankruptcy after one year?
cards.b: Under Insolvency Act 1986 s335A(3), the court assumes the creditors' interests outweigh all other considerations unless the circumstances are exceptional.

cards.f: What is the maximum number of legal owners of land?
cards.b: Four (Trustee Act 1925 s34; LPA s34). They always hold the legal title as joint tenants, which cannot be severed.

cards.f: What happens to the shares when one of three beneficial joint tenants severs?
cards.b: The severing party becomes a tenant in common of a one-third share. The other two remain joint tenants of the remaining two-thirds as between themselves.

cards.f: What are the hallmarks of a tenancy according to Street v Mountford [1985]?
cards.b: Exclusive possession, for a term, at a rent. A label calling the agreement a licence does not alter that result.

cards.f: Why were the occupiers in Antoniades v Villiers [1990] tenants?
cards.b: The clause letting the landlord share the small flat with others was a sham, never intended to be used. The couple had joint exclusive possession.

cards.f: Why were the occupiers in AG Securities v Vaughan [1990] licensees?
cards.b: They signed separate agreements at different times and for different sums. Without the four unities they could not hold exclusive possession jointly.

cards.f: What did Mexfield v Berrisford [2011] decide?
cards.b: A tenancy of uncertain duration granted to an individual took effect as a lease for life. LPA s149(6) turned it into a 90-year term that ends on death.

cards.f: What is a Bruton tenancy?
cards.b: A non-proprietary, contractual tenancy recognised in Bruton v London & Quadrant [2000]. It binds the parties to each other, even though the grantor had no estate to grant.

cards.f: Under the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995, what happens to the original tenant on assignment?
cards.b: For leases granted from 1996 the tenant is released from the covenants on a lawful assignment (s5), but may have to enter an authorised guarantee agreement guaranteeing the assignee (s16).

cards.f: What must a landlord do before forfeiting for a breach other than non-payment of rent?
cards.b: Serve an LPA s146 notice that identifies the breach, requires it to be remedied if it can be, and asks for compensation if wanted. The tenant may apply for relief.

cards.f: How can a landlord waive the right to forfeit?
cards.b: By an unequivocal act that recognises the lease continues, such as demanding or accepting rent, while knowing of the breach.

cards.f: Which leases must be registered to be legal under the LRA 2002?
cards.b: Leases granted for more than seven years (s27(2)(b)). Legal leases of seven years or less override under Sch 3 para 1.

cards.f: Which test applies to covenants in leases granted before 1996?
cards.b: Covenants run with the lease and reversion if they touch and concern the land (have reference to the subject matter of the lease). The original parties stay liable through privity of contract.

cards.f: List the Re Ellenborough Park [1956] characteristics.
cards.b: A dominant and a servient tenement; the right must accommodate the dominant tenement; the two must be owned or occupied by different people; and the right must be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant.

cards.f: Why was the right in Hill v Tupper (1863) not an easement?
cards.b: The exclusive right to put pleasure boats on a canal was a commercial monopoly benefiting the business. It did not benefit the land itself.

cards.f: Which three conditions apply under Wheeldon v Burrows (1879)?
cards.b: The quasi-easement must have been continuous and apparent, necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the land granted, and in use at the time of the grant.

cards.f: How can LPA 1925 s62 create an easement?
cards.b: A conveyance passes rights enjoyed with the land, so a licence or quasi-easement can be upgraded into a legal easement (Wright v Macadam [1949]).

cards.f: Is diversity of occupation always needed under s62?
cards.b: No. Long v Gowlett [1923] required it, but Platt v Crouch [2003] and Wood v Waddington [2015] held it unnecessary where the right was continuous and apparent.

cards.f: What did Regency Villas v Diamond Resorts [2018] decide?
cards.b: Purely recreational and sporting rights, such as using a swimming pool and golf course, can be easements if they meet the Ellenborough Park requirements.

cards.f: What does use "as of right" mean for prescription?
cards.b: Use without force, without secrecy and without permission (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario), carried on for 20 years.

cards.f: When will an implied legal easement override a registered disposition?
cards.b: Under LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 3, only if the purchaser actually knew of it, it was obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, or it had been exercised in the year before the disposition.

cards.f: What principle does Copeland v Greenhalf [1952] illustrate?
cards.b: A right that effectively gives the claimant exclusive or joint possession of the servient land, there storage of vehicles over a strip, cannot be an easement.

cards.f: When is an easement implied by necessity?
cards.b: Only where the land granted or retained could not be used at all without the easement, for example a landlocked plot. Convenience is not enough.

cards.f: What did Rhone v Stephens [1994] confirm?
cards.b: The burden of a positive freehold covenant, there to repair a roof, does not run at law or in equity to successors of the covenantor.

cards.f: What are the requirements for the burden to run under Tulk v Moxhay (1848)?
cards.b: The covenant must be negative in substance, it must benefit land the covenantee retained, the parties must have intended it to run, and the successor must be bound under the priority rules.

cards.f: Why did the burden fail in LCC v Allen [1914]?
cards.b: The covenantee held no land that the covenant benefited, so a restrictive covenant could not bind the covenantor's successors in equity.

cards.f: What did Federated Homes v Mill Lodge [1980] decide about s78?
cards.b: LPA s78 automatically annexes the benefit of a covenant that touches and concerns the land to each and every part of the covenantee's land.

cards.f: Which limit on Federated Homes did Crest Nicholson v McAllister [2004] add?
cards.b: Statutory annexation under s78 only works where the benefited land can be identified from the conveyance, read with the surrounding circumstances. It can also be excluded expressly.

cards.f: What is the benefit and burden principle?
cards.b: A successor who takes a benefit under a deed must take on a burden that is reciprocal and relevant to it, provided they have a real choice whether to take the benefit (Halsall v Brizell [1957]; Thamesmead v Allotey (1998)).

cards.f: What are the requirements of a scheme of development under Elliston v Reacher [1908]?
cards.b: Title derived from a common seller; the estate laid out in lots before the sales; covenants intended to benefit all lots; purchasers buying on that footing; and in modern cases a clearly defined area.

cards.f: How is a restrictive covenant protected in registered land?
cards.b: By entering a notice on the register of the burdened title. Otherwise a purchaser for value takes free under LRA 2002 s29.

cards.f: Under which section can the Upper Tribunal discharge or modify restrictive covenants?
cards.b: LPA 1925 s84, on grounds including obsolescence and the covenant impeding a reasonable use of the land.

cards.f: How do you tell whether a covenant is negative in substance?
cards.b: Ask whether the covenantor must spend money or take positive action to comply. If so it is positive, however it is worded.

cards.f: What principle did Samuel v Jarrah Timber [1904] apply?
cards.b: An option for the mortgagee to buy the mortgaged property, granted in the mortgage itself, is a void clog on the equity of redemption.

cards.f: When are collateral advantages valid?
cards.b: When they are not unfair or unconscionable and are not in the nature of a penalty clogging the equity of redemption (Kreglinger v New Patagonia Meat [1914]). In Kreglinger itself an option over sheepskins that continued after redemption was upheld, because it was a separate collateral bargain.

cards.f: What does the Administration of Justice Act 1970 s36 allow?
cards.b: Where a lender seeks possession of a dwelling-house, the court can adjourn or suspend the order if the borrower is likely to pay the sums due within a reasonable period.

cards.f: What starting point for a reasonable period did Cheltenham & Gloucester v Norgan [1996] set?
cards.b: The court should take the full remaining term of the mortgage as its starting point when deciding the period over which the arrears can be repaid.

cards.f: What duty does a mortgagee owe when selling?
cards.b: To take reasonable care to obtain the true market value on the date of sale (Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance [1971]). It may choose when to sell (Silven Properties v RBS [2003]).

cards.f: When is a lender put on inquiry under Etridge (No 2) [2001]?
cards.b: Whenever the relationship between the surety and the debtor is non-commercial, for example when a wife guarantees her husband's business debts.

cards.f: When does a mortgagee's power of sale arise, and when does it become exercisable?
cards.b: It arises under LPA s101 once the legal redemption date has passed. It becomes exercisable under s103 after a notice requiring repayment plus three months' default, interest two months in arrears, or a breach of another term.

cards.f: When may a mortgagee take possession?
cards.b: As soon as the mortgage is made, even without default, unless the mortgage terms exclude this (Four-Maids v Dudley Marshall [1957]).

cards.f: What happens to any surplus after a mortgagee's sale?
cards.b: Under LPA s105 the mortgagee holds it on trust to pay subsequent encumbrancers and then the mortgagor.

cards.f: Why is Palk v Mortgage Services Funding [1993] notable?
cards.b: The court used LPA s91 to order a sale at the borrower's request against the lender's wishes, because negative equity was growing.

cards.f: What are the two elements of adverse possession according to Pye v Graham [2002]?
cards.b: Factual possession (an appropriate degree of physical control) and an intention to possess (to exclude the world, including the paper owner, so far as reasonably practicable).

cards.f: After how long can a squatter of registered land apply to be registered?
cards.b: After 10 years' adverse possession ending on the date of the application (LRA 2002 Sch 6 para 1).

cards.f: What are the three para 5 conditions in Sch 6?
cards.b: Estoppel; some other entitlement to be registered; and a boundary case, where the squatter reasonably believed for 10 years that the land belonged to them.

cards.f: What happens if the registered owner does not evict the squatter after a counter-notice?
cards.b: If the squatter remains in adverse possession for two more years, they may reapply and are entitled to be registered (Sch 6 paras 6–7).

cards.f: What did Best v Chief Land Registrar [2015] decide?
cards.b: The criminal offence of squatting in a residential building (LASPO 2012 s144) does not prevent adverse possession from counting towards a claim.

cards.f: What are the elements of proprietary estoppel?
cards.b: An assurance or encouragement, reliance on it, detriment, and unconscionability in going back on it. The court then decides how to satisfy the equity.

cards.f: Why did the claim in Thorner v Major [2009] succeed?
cards.b: Oblique remarks over many years were clear enough in their context to amount to an assurance that the farm would pass to the claimant, who worked on it unpaid in reliance.

cards.f: Why did the claim in Cobbe v Yeoman's Row [2008] fail?
cards.b: The claimant knew there was no binding agreement and was taking a commercial risk. An expectation of a future contract is not a belief in a proprietary right.

cards.f: What approach to remedy did Guest v Guest [2022] adopt?
cards.b: The court starts from fulfilling the promised expectation, then considers whether that would be disproportionate, adjusting for factors such as accelerated receipt of the benefit.

cards.f: Does an equity by estoppel bind third parties in registered land?
cards.b: Yes. Under LRA 2002 s116 it is proprietary from the time it arises. It needs a notice, or it can override if the claimant is in actual occupation.

questions.q: Which of the following can exist as a legal estate under LPA 1925 s1(1)?
options: A life interest
A term of years absolute
A fee tail
A beneficial interest under a trust
questions.why: Only the fee simple absolute in possession and the term of years absolute can be legal estates. Life interests and entails are equitable only.

questions.q: A seller and buyer sign separate copies of a written agreement to sell a house, but a term agreeing that the carpets will be included was agreed orally and left out. What is the most likely position under LP(MP)A 1989 s2?
options: The contract is valid, and the carpets term is unenforceable
The contract is void because it does not contain all the expressly agreed terms, unless rectification or a collateral contract can save it
The contract is valid because exchanging signed copies satisfies s2
The contract is voidable at the buyer's option
questions.why: Section 2 requires all expressly agreed terms to be in the document. Omitting one makes the contract void, although rectification or a separate collateral contract may sometimes save it.

questions.q: Under LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 1, which leases override a registered disposition?
options: Equitable leases of any length
Legal leases granted for seven years or less
Legal leases granted for more than seven years
Any lease in writing
questions.why: Para 1 covers legal leases of seven years or less (with limited exceptions). Longer leases must be registered.

questions.q: R holds a beneficial interest in a registered house owned by S. R lives there but is abroad on a long working trip when S mortgages the house to Bank X, and R's clothes and furniture remain in the house. Which is the best view?
options: R cannot be in actual occupation while physically absent
R may still be in actual occupation if there is continuing physical evidence of occupation and an intention to return, as in Link Lending v Bustard
R's interest automatically binds the bank under s28
R's interest is overreached because the bank paid S
questions.why: Temporary absence does not necessarily end actual occupation where there are physical signs of occupation and an intention to return. Overreaching needs payment to two trustees, and S is a sole trustee.

questions.q: A and B are beneficial joint tenants. A posts a notice of severance to B's home under LPA s36(2). B never reads it, and A dies the next day after changing her mind. Which is correct?
options: No severance, because B never read the notice
No severance, because A changed her mind before B read it
Severance occurred once the notice was delivered to B's home
Severance only occurs if the notice is registered
questions.why: Kinch v Bullard [1999]: service by delivery to the last known address under LPA s196 is effective, whether or not the notice is read.

questions.q: In Street v Mountford [1985], which factor was decisive in finding a tenancy?
options: The parties' description of the agreement as a licence
The grant of exclusive possession for a term at a rent
The fact that the occupier paid a premium
The occupier's intention to stay permanently
questions.why: Lord Templeman held that exclusive possession for a term at a rent creates a tenancy, apart from exceptional cases. Labels are not decisive.

questions.q: On selling part of her land, a seller reserves (rather than grants) a right of way over the part sold. If no express reservation is made, which route to an implied easement is available to the seller?
options: The rule in Wheeldon v Burrows
LPA 1925 s62
Necessity or common intention
All of the above
questions.why: Wheeldon v Burrows and s62 operate only in favour of a grantee. A seller who fails to reserve an easement expressly must rely on necessity or common intention, which the courts construe strictly against the grantor.

questions.q: Which case established that the burden of a restrictive freehold covenant can run in equity?
options: Austerberry v Oldham Corporation
Tulk v Moxhay
Rhone v Stephens
Federated Homes v Mill Lodge
questions.why: Tulk v Moxhay (1848) allowed equity to enforce a restrictive covenant against a successor with notice. Austerberry and Rhone concern the non-running of positive burdens.

questions.q: In a mortgage deed, a lender takes an option to buy the mortgaged property at a fixed price within five years. What is the most likely result?
options: The option is valid if the price is fair
The option is void as a clog on the equity of redemption
The option is valid only between commercial parties
The whole mortgage is void
questions.why: Samuel v Jarrah Timber [1904]: an option to purchase in the mortgage transaction itself is void because it could prevent redemption. The rest of the mortgage stands.

questions.q: In a Sch 6 LRA 2002 application, a squatter has occupied a strip of land next to her garden for 11 years, believing reasonably throughout that it was hers. The registered owner serves a counter-notice. Which para 5 condition is most relevant?
options: Estoppel
Some other right to the land
The boundary condition
None, because a counter-notice defeats every application
questions.why: Para 5(4) applies where land adjoins the squatter's own, the exact boundary has not been fixed, and the squatter reasonably believed for at least 10 years ending on the date of the application that the land was theirs.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a fixture and a chattel, and identify the test courts use to tell them apart.
markScheme: A fixture becomes part of the land and passes with it; a chattel remains personal property
Holland v Hodgson: degree of annexation
Object or purpose of annexation is the more important factor
Illustration from case law (eg Elitestone v Morris or Botham v TSB)
questions.modelAnswer: A fixture is an item that has become part of the land, so it passes to a buyer unless it is excluded. A chattel stays personal property and can be removed. Holland v Hodgson (1872) asks first how firmly the item is attached, which creates a presumption, and then why it was attached. Purpose is now the decisive question: was the item fixed to improve the land permanently, or to enjoy it better as a chattel? In Elitestone v Morris [1997] a bungalow that could not be removed without being destroyed was part of the land. In Botham v TSB [1996] carpets and appliances were chattels.

questions.q: Explain how overreaching protects a purchaser of registered land held on trust, and its limits.
markScheme: LPA ss2 and 27: payment of capital money to at least two trustees or a trust corporation
Beneficial interests detach from the land and attach to the proceeds
Applies even against beneficiaries in actual occupation (Flegg)
No overreaching where there is a sole trustee, so Boland-type actual occupation can bind
A restriction on the register directs that two trustees must receive the money
questions.modelAnswer: Overreaching under LPA ss2 and 27 lets a buyer take free of beneficial interests under a trust of land if the purchase money is paid to at least two trustees or a trust corporation. The interests do not disappear. They attach to the money instead of the land. In City of London BS v Flegg [1988] this defeated beneficiaries who were in actual occupation. The limit is that a single trustee cannot give a valid receipt. Where one person holds the legal title, a beneficiary in actual occupation can bind the buyer, as in Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland [1981]. A Form A restriction tells buyers about the two-trustee requirement.

questions.q: Pat, Quinn and Rory buy a house as beneficial joint tenants. Pat later mortgages her interest to a lender to fund her business. Rory then dies, leaving his estate to his sister. Explain who owns what in equity.
markScheme: A mortgage of one joint tenant's interest is an act operating on her share, which severs (Williams v Hensman; First National Security v Hegerty)
Pat becomes a tenant in common of one-third, subject to the mortgage
Quinn and Rory remain joint tenants of two-thirds as between themselves
On Rory's death survivorship gives Quinn the two-thirds, so Rory's sister takes nothing
questions.modelAnswer: Pat's mortgage of her own beneficial interest is an act operating on her share, one of the Williams v Hensman methods, so it severs her interest (see also First National Security v Hegerty [1985]). She now holds a one-third share as a tenant in common, subject to the lender's charge. Quinn and Rory are still joint tenants of the remaining two-thirds as between themselves. When Rory dies, survivorship applies, so his share goes to Quinn and not under his will. In equity, Quinn now holds two-thirds and Pat one-third. Pat and Quinn hold the legal title on trust.

questions.q: Distinguish a lease from a licence and explain why the distinction matters.
markScheme: Lease = exclusive possession for a term at a rent (Street v Mountford)
A lease is a proprietary estate capable of binding successors; a licence is personal
Exceptions such as no intention to create legal relations, service occupancy and lodgers
Sham clauses are ignored (Antoniades v Villiers)
questions.modelAnswer: Under Street v Mountford [1985] a lease is the grant of exclusive possession for a term, usually at a rent. A licence is only a personal permission to be on the land. The distinction matters because a lease is a proprietary estate. It can bind buyers of the freehold, it can be assigned, and it attracts statutory protection for residential and business tenants. A licence binds only the parties. Exclusive possession does not create a tenancy where there is no intention to create legal relations, where the occupier is a service occupier, or where the occupier is a lodger. Courts disregard sham terms, as in Antoniades v Villiers [1990].

questions.q: Explain the requirement that an easement must "accommodate" the dominant tenement.
markScheme: The right must benefit the land itself, not merely the owner personally
Proximity: the tenements need not adjoin but must be close enough
Business benefits count only if they are connected with normal use of the land (Hill v Tupper contrasted with Moody v Steggles)
Ellenborough Park: use of a garden enhanced the houses as residences
questions.modelAnswer: To accommodate the dominant tenement, the right must benefit the land and its normal use, so that it would also benefit any later owner. It must not simply give a personal or commercial advantage to the current owner. The tenements do not have to adjoin, but they must be close enough. In Hill v Tupper (1863) a monopoly over pleasure boating benefited a business, not the land. In Moody v Steggles (1879), however, a right to hang a pub sign on neighbouring land was valid, because the land was used as a pub. In Re Ellenborough Park [1956] the right to use a communal garden benefited the houses as homes.

questions.q: Explain why the burden of a positive freehold covenant does not run, and identify two ways in which conveyancers try to work around this.
markScheme: Austerberry v Oldham: burden does not run at common law (no privity)
Equity will not enforce a positive obligation against a successor: Rhone v Stephens
Workaround 1: chain of indemnity covenants
Workaround 2: benefit and burden principle (Halsall v Brizell), long lease, estate rentcharge or commonhold
questions.modelAnswer: At common law only the parties to a contract are bound by it, so a covenant's burden cannot pass with freehold land (Austerberry v Oldham (1885)). Equity relaxed this in Tulk v Moxhay, but only for negative covenants, because enforcing them simply restrains the use of land. In Rhone v Stephens [1994] the House of Lords refused to extend Tulk to positive covenants, since that would force successors to spend money under promises they never made. One workaround is a chain of indemnity covenants, where each buyer promises the seller to perform and to obtain the same promise on resale. Another is Halsall v Brizell: paying for a road is tied to using it.

questions.q: Explain how the court's powers under the Administration of Justice Act 1970 s36 protect residential borrowers.
markScheme: Applies where the mortgagee seeks possession of a dwelling-house
Court may adjourn, stay, suspend or postpone if the borrower is likely to pay sums due within a reasonable period
AJA 1973 s8: 'sums due' means arrears, not the whole accelerated debt
Norgan: start from the remaining mortgage term
No power where the lender takes peaceable possession without a court order (Ropaigealach)
questions.modelAnswer: Section 36 applies where a lender seeks possession of a dwelling-house. The court can adjourn the proceedings or suspend or postpone the order if the borrower is likely to be able to pay the sums due within a reasonable period. Under AJA 1973 s8, the sums due are the arrears rather than the whole debt that becomes payable on default. Cheltenham & Gloucester v Norgan [1996] makes the full remaining term the starting point for that period. There are limits. The borrower needs a realistic, evidenced plan. Ropaigealach v Barclays [2000] held that s36 does not apply if the lender takes possession peaceably without going to court.

questions.q: Outline the elements of a proprietary estoppel claim.
markScheme: Assurance: clear enough in context (Thorner v Major)
Reliance on the assurance
Detriment, assessed in the round (Gillett v Holt)
Unconscionability ties the elements together and justifies a remedy
Court decides the minimum equity / how to satisfy it (Guest v Guest)
questions.modelAnswer: Proprietary estoppel needs an assurance, reliance, detriment and unconscionability. The assurance must be clear enough in its context and does not have to be express. Thorner v Major [2009] accepted remarks made obliquely over many years. The claimant must have relied on the assurance and suffered detriment. Gillett v Holt [2001] assesses detriment across the whole course of dealing, setting it against any benefits received. It must also be unconscionable for the person who made the assurance to go back on it. Once an equity arises, the court decides how to satisfy it. Under Guest v Guest [2022] the starting point is fulfilling the expectation, then adjusting for proportionality.

questions.q: Explain why Abbey National v Cann [1991] matters for occupiers claiming overriding interests, especially where a purchase is funded by a mortgage.
markScheme: Actual occupation is judged at completion (date of disposition)
Fleeting preparatory acts (carpet-laying) are not occupation
Scintilla temporis rejected: purchase and mortgage are one indivisible transaction
So the purchaser has nothing out of which to grant an interest that beats the acquisition mortgagee
Applied under the LRA 2002 by Scott v Southern Pacific Mortgages [2014]
questions.modelAnswer: Cann holds that actual occupation is tested at completion. Preparatory acts, such as laying carpets shortly before completion, do not count. More importantly, the House of Lords rejected the scintilla temporis argument. When a buyer uses a mortgage to buy, the conveyance and the charge are one indivisible transaction. The buyer never holds an unencumbered estate, even for a moment, out of which an earlier interest could be granted with priority over the acquisition lender. The occupier's interest is therefore subject to that mortgage. The Supreme Court applied this reasoning to registered land under the 2002 Act in Scott v Southern Pacific Mortgages [2014], where sellers in sale-and-leaseback schemes lost out to the lenders.

questions.q: Explain the significance of Mexfield Housing Co-operative v Berrisford [2011] for the certainty of term rule.
markScheme: Rule: the maximum duration must be certain at the outset (Lace v Chantler; Prudential v LRB)
Agreement was terminable only on specified events, so the term was uncertain
At common law, an uncertain term granted to an individual took effect as a lease for life
LPA s149(6) converts it into a 90-year term determinable on death
Supreme Court criticised the rule but felt unable to abolish it
questions.modelAnswer: The certainty rule requires the maximum length of a lease to be known when it starts (Lace v Chantler [1944]; Prudential v London Residuary Body [1992]). In Mexfield, the occupancy agreement allowed the co-operative to end it only on specified grounds such as arrears, so its maximum length was uncertain. The Supreme Court held that, before 1926, a tenancy of uncertain duration granted to an individual would have been treated as a lease for life. LPA s149(6) now converts such a lease into a 90-year term that ends on the tenant's death, and the agreed termination events still apply. The Court criticised the certainty rule as lacking any satisfactory rationale but did not overrule it.

questions.q: Hana buys "Orchard House", a registered freehold, from Ivo. Before completion Ivo removes: (a) a heavy marble statue of a stag resting on its own weight in the centre of a formal garden designed around it; (b) fitted kitchen units screwed to the walls; (c) a free-standing American-style fridge; and (d) a summerhouse bolted to a concrete base, which can be unbolted and moved in a day. Ivo had also agreed in an email with Hana that she could have the garden furniture, but this was not included in the signed contract. Advise Hana.
markScheme: Explain the fixtures/chattels distinction and that fixtures pass on a sale unless excluded (LPA s62 also passes fixtures)
Holland v Hodgson two-stage test; object of annexation is decisive
Statue: resting by its own weight suggests a chattel, but an integral part of the garden design suggests a fixture (D'Eyncourt v Gregory)
Kitchen units: fixed and intended to improve the building, so fixtures
Fridge: free-standing appliance, chattel (Botham v TSB)
Summerhouse: consider Elitestone; easily removable and bolted down for stability, probably a chattel, but arguable
Garden furniture: a chattel, so it does not pass under the land contract
LP(MP)A 1989 s2: an omitted agreed term may make the land contract void unless it is a separate collateral contract
Remedies: damages for breach/conversion for wrongly removed fixtures
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Fixtures form part of the land and pass to a buyer unless the contract excludes them. Chattels do not pass. Holland v Hodgson (1872) asks about the degree of annexation, which creates a presumption, and then about the object of annexation, which is decisive.

(a) The statue rests under its own weight, so it is presumed to be a chattel. However, in D'Eyncourt v Gregory (1866) statues that formed part of an architectural design were held to be fixtures. Since this garden was laid out around the stag, Hana has a strong argument that it was meant to be a permanent improvement to the land. If so, removing it was a breach of contract.

(b) The kitchen units are fixed to the walls and fitted to improve the building as a house. They are fixtures, so Hana can claim their value or the cost of reinstatement.

(c) The fridge is free-standing and is used as an appliance. It is a chattel (Botham v TSB [1996]), and Ivo may take it.

(d) The summerhouse is harder. It is bolted down, so the presumption favours a fixture. But the bolts may serve only to keep it stable, and it can be moved without damage, unlike the bungalow in Elitestone v Morris [1997]. On balance it is probably a chattel unless it was integral to the garden's design.

The garden furniture is a chattel, so the land contract would not transfer it anyway. The term was agreed but left out of the signed document. That raises s2 of the LP(MP)A 1989, which requires all expressly agreed terms to be included. If the furniture term was part of the land deal, the contract could be void. The better analysis is that it was a separate collateral contract for goods, which need not meet s2, so Hana can enforce it. Rectification is another possibility.

Hana should claim damages for the kitchen units and probably the statue. She may also have a contractual claim for the furniture.

questions.q: Dev is the sole registered proprietor of "Larches". His partner, Esme, contributed a third of the purchase price, and she lives there with him. Dev's father, Fergus, lives in a converted garage in the grounds and paid for the conversion on Dev's oral promise that he could live there for life. Dev's neighbour, Gita, has a 10-year lease of the paddock, which was never registered. Dev has also granted his brother a right of way over the drive by a signed letter. Dev sells Larches to Hugo, who pays Dev alone and registers the transfer. Hugo did not inspect the garage. Advise Hugo.
markScheme: Hugo is a purchaser for value whose transfer is registered, so s29 applies: he takes free of everything except notices and Sch 3 interests
Esme: resulting/common intention constructive trust interest; no overreaching as there was one trustee
Esme in actual occupation: Sch 3 para 2 (Boland); consider inquiry and disclosure
Fergus: equity by estoppel (s116) is capable of overriding if he is in actual occupation
Fergus: is his occupation obvious on a reasonably careful inspection? Hugo's failure to inspect is not a defence if it was obvious
Gita: a 10-year lease must be registered (s27), so it takes effect only in equity; not para 1
But Gita may override under para 2 if she is in actual occupation of the paddock (consider the nature of the land)
Brother: the letter is not a deed, so the right can only be an equitable easement at most if s2 is satisfied; it needs a notice and does not fall within para 3
Brother's easement probably does not bind Hugo
Conclusion and remedies (indemnity unlikely; Hugo's claims against Dev)
questions.modelAnswer:
Hugo bought for value and has registered the transfer, so under LRA 2002 s29 he takes free of earlier interests unless they are protected by a notice or are overriding under Schedule 3. Nothing is noted, so Schedule 3 is key.

Esme. Her contribution gives her a beneficial interest under a resulting or common intention constructive trust. Hugo paid Dev alone, a sole trustee, so the interest was not overreached (LPA ss2 and 27). She lives at Larches, so she is in actual occupation and her interest overrides under para 2, as in Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland [1981]. It would fail only if Hugo had asked her about her rights and she had not disclosed them, and nothing suggests he did.

Fergus. Dev's assurance, together with Fergus paying for the conversion, probably gives Fergus an equity by estoppel. Under s116 that equity is proprietary from the moment it arises. Fergus lives in the garage, so he is in actual occupation. Hugo's failure to inspect does not help him. Para 2(c) asks whether the occupation would have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, and a lived-in converted garage almost certainly would have been. Fergus's equity therefore binds Hugo, and the court will decide how to satisfy it, for example with a right to occupy or a money payment.

Gita. A lease of more than seven years must be registered to be legal (s27(2)(b)), so Gita has only an equitable lease under Walsh v Lonsdale, which falls outside para 1. Para 2 may still protect her if she is in actual occupation of the paddock, for example through regular grazing, which suits land of that kind.

The brother. The letter is not a deed, so the right of way is at most an equitable easement, and only if the letter meets s2. Para 3 covers only legal easements, and no notice was entered, so the right does not bind Hugo.

Hugo is therefore bound by Esme's interest and Fergus's equity, and probably by Gita's lease. He may sue Dev on the title guarantee.

questions.q: Ina, Jon and Kat bought a house in 2015, registered in their three names. The transfer contained no declaration of trust. Ina paid 50% of the price and Jon and Kat 25% each. All three ran a yoga business from the ground floor. In 2023 Jon told the others over dinner that he wanted to "cash out" and they agreed to buy him out for £100,000, but no paperwork followed. In 2025 Jon died, leaving everything to his son. Kat now wants the house sold; Ina, whose disabled daughter lives there, refuses. Advise the parties.
markScheme: Legal title: Ina, Jon and Kat as joint tenants on trust; on Jon's death the legal title passes to Ina and Kat by survivorship
Beneficial interests: no express declaration; consider presumptions in equity
Business use and unequal contributions suggest a tenancy in common (Malayan Credit); contrast the Stack/Jones presumption for domestic joint names
If tenancy in common: shares 50/25/25 and Jon's share passes under his will
If joint tenancy: consider severance by mutual agreement (Burgess v Rawnsley), which need not be enforceable
Consider also course of dealing; s36(2) notice absent
Result for Jon's son
TOLATA s14 application by Kat; s15 factors including the welfare of a minor (if the daughter is a minor) and the purpose of the trust
Purpose (business plus home) may have ended; court's discretion (Mortgage Corp v Shaire)
Alternatives: order sale, postpone sale, or allow a buy-out
questions.modelAnswer:
Legal title. The three registered owners held the legal estate as joint tenants on a trust of land. Survivorship always applies at law, so on Jon's death the legal title vested in Ina and Kat as trustees.

Beneficial interests. There was no express declaration of trust, so Goodman v Gallant [1986] does not settle the matter. For a domestic home in joint names, Stack v Dowden [2007] and Jones v Kernott [2011] start from a beneficial joint tenancy. This property, however, was partly a business asset. Malayan Credit v Jack Chia [1986] shows that equity presumes a tenancy in common between business associates and where contributions are unequal. On that basis the shares are 50%, 25% and 25%, and Jon's quarter passed under his will to his son.

Even if there was a beneficial joint tenancy, the 2023 agreement probably severed it. In Burgess v Rawnsley [1975], an informal agreement for one co-owner to buy out another severed the joint tenancy, even though it was unenforceable and later fell through. Severance by mutual agreement needs no writing and no s36(2) notice. Either way, Jon's son probably holds a quarter share, and Ina and Kat hold the legal title on trust for all three of them.

Sale. Kat, or the son, may apply under TOLATA s14. The court will weigh the s15 factors. The purpose of the trust, a business and possibly a home, may have ended with Jon's death. Under s15(1)(c) the court must consider the welfare of any minor in occupation, but that applies only if Ina's daughter is under 18. If she is an adult, her disability is still relevant as part of the general circumstances. Mortgage Corp v Shaire [2001] confirms that the court has a wide discretion. The possible orders include an immediate sale, a postponed sale to give the daughter time to rehouse, or an order allowing Ina to buy out the others at valuation. A buy-out would respect both her larger share and her family's needs.

questions.q: Lark Properties owns a block of studio flats. It lets Flat 4 to Mo and Nia, a couple, under two identical "licence agreements" signed on the same day, each requiring £600 a month and stating that the owner may introduce further occupiers. The studio has one bed. Lark also lets a shop to Odile for 5 years by a signed written agreement (not a deed) from 2022; Odile later assigns to Pip without the landlord's consent, contrary to a covenant. Pip has breached a covenant to repair. Advise Lark on (a) the status of Mo and Nia and (b) its rights against Odile and Pip.
markScheme: Street v Mountford: exclusive possession, term, rent creates a tenancy
Sham/pretence clause: Antoniades v Villiers; the one-bed studio makes sharing unrealistic
Joint tenancy needs the four unities; signed on the same day for equal sums, so they can be joint tenants; contrast AG Securities v Vaughan
Consequence: residential tenancy; possession only through court (PEA 1977); note the Renters' Rights Act 2025 regime
Odile: a 5-year lease not by deed is not within s54(2) (over 3 years), so it is an equitable lease under Walsh v Lonsdale
Lease granted after 1995, so LT(C)A 1995 applies (it covers equitable leases)
Assignment in breach of covenant is an excluded assignment (s11): Odile is not released and remains liable
Pip is bound by the tenant covenants (s3) and liable for the disrepair
Remedies: forfeiture (needs a re-entry clause; s146 notice; Leasehold Property (Repairs) Act 1938 where applicable), damages; waiver risk
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Mo and Nia. Under Street v Mountford [1985], exclusive possession for a term at a rent creates a tenancy, whatever label is used. In Antoniades v Villiers [1990], a clause allowing the owner to introduce other occupiers into a small flat shared by a couple was held to be a sham. A one-bed studio cannot realistically be shared with strangers, so this clause is probably a sham too. That leaves Mo and Nia with exclusive possession together. A joint tenancy also needs the four unities. Their agreements were signed on the same day, on identical terms and for equal sums. That distinguishes AG Securities v Vaughan [1990], where the agreements were made at different times for different rents, so these can be read together as one joint letting. Mo and Nia are probably joint tenants. Lark can recover possession only through the courts (Protection from Eviction Act 1977). Under the Renters' Rights Act 2025 no-fault possession is no longer available, so Lark will need a statutory ground.

(b) Odile and Pip. A five-year term is longer than three years, so s54(2) does not apply, and without a deed the lease cannot be legal. A signed written agreement that meets s2, however, gives Odile an equitable lease under Walsh v Lonsdale (1882). The lease was granted after 1995, so the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 applies, and it covers equitable leases. Odile assigned without the consent the lease required, which makes the assignment an excluded assignment under s11. Odile is therefore not released under s5. Pip is bound by the tenant covenants under s3 and is liable for the disrepair, and Odile is liable alongside Pip.

Remedies. Lark can claim damages for the disrepair, limited by the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927 s18. If the lease has a re-entry clause, Lark can also forfeit after serving a s146 notice, and Pip may apply for relief. Lark must not accept rent knowing of the breaches, because that would waive its right to forfeit.

questions.q: Quill owned two adjoining houses, Rose Cottage and Sage Lodge. While she lived in Sage Lodge, she let Rose Cottage to Tam, permitting him informally to use a path across Sage Lodge's garden to reach the bus stop and to store his bicycles in her garden shed. In 2024 Quill sold the freehold of Rose Cottage to Tam by a transfer that said nothing about either right. Quill also used a drain under Rose Cottage serving Sage Lodge. Quill has now sold Sage Lodge to Uma, who has locked the gate and the shed. Advise Tam and Uma.
markScheme: Ellenborough Park characteristics for each right
Path: accommodates Rose Cottage; capable of grant
Shed storage: exclusive use, so likely to fail (Copeland v Greenhalf; Batchelor v Marlow); consider Moncrieff's reasonable-use test
Section 62: the transfer converts the existing licence into a legal easement; diversity of occupation existed (Tam was the tenant)
Wright v Macadam: s62 applied to a permissive storage right (coal shed)
Wheeldon v Burrows as an alternative for the path: continuous and apparent? necessary for reasonable enjoyment?
Drain: a reservation in favour of Quill; Wheeldon and s62 do not apply; necessity or common intention (Pwllbach); construed strictly
Binding effect on Uma: Tam's benefit attached to his land; the burden runs with Sage Lodge
Implied legal easements bind Uma as a registered purchaser under Sch 3 para 3 if they were obvious, known, or used within the year
Conclusion and remedies (injunction, damages)
questions.modelAnswer:
Tam's path. A route to the bus stop benefits Rose Cottage as a home and meets the Re Ellenborough Park [1956] requirements. Before 2024 it was only a licence. Under LPA 1925 s62, a conveyance passes the rights enjoyed with the land at the time. Quill and Tam occupied the two properties separately, so the diversity of occupation required by Long v Gowlett [1923] is present. Wright v Macadam [1949] confirms that s62 can upgrade a permissive right into a legal easement, and the transfer did not exclude s62. Tam therefore has a legal easement of way. Wheeldon v Burrows (1879) is a weaker alternative, because a garden path may not be continuous and apparent.

Bicycle storage. Wright v Macadam itself upheld a right to store coal in a shed. But if Tam used the whole shed and kept Quill out, the right amounts to exclusive use. Such a right cannot exist as an easement (Copeland v Greenhalf [1952]; Batchelor v Marlow [2003]). Moncrieff v Jamieson [2007] asks instead whether the servient owner keeps reasonable use of the land. The storage claim is strong only if Tam's use was shared or limited.

Quill's drain. Quill kept Sage Lodge, so any drainage right would have been reserved, not granted. Wheeldon v Burrows and s62 help only grantees. Quill, and now Uma, must show necessity or common intention (Pwllbach Colliery v Woodman [1915]), and the courts construe these strictly against a grantor. Draining an existing house may reflect the parties' shared intention, so Uma has an arguable claim, which also gives her bargaining leverage.

Who is bound. Easements arising by implication or under s62 are legal but unregistered. They bind a registered buyer under LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 3 if the buyer knew of them, they were obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, or they were used in the year before the sale. A worn path with a gate, in regular use, satisfies this. Tam can seek an injunction requiring Uma to unlock the gate, and damages.

questions.q: In 2010 Vera sold part of her land, keeping "Willow Farm", to Wes. Wes covenanted, "for the benefit of Vera's adjoining land", (i) not to build more than one dwelling on the plot and (ii) to maintain the boundary hedge. The covenants were protected by notice. Wes sold to Xander in 2018; Xander now plans a second house and has grubbed up the hedge. Vera sold part of Willow Farm to Yasmin in 2020; the transfer said nothing about the covenants. Xander shared Vera's private road throughout, under a deed requiring road users to contribute to upkeep. Discuss who can enforce what against whom, and whether the law here is satisfactory.
markScheme: Separate benefit and burden, at law and in equity
Covenant (i) is negative in substance; the burden runs under Tulk v Moxhay: the covenantee had retained land, there was intention (s79), and it was protected by notice
Covenant (ii) is positive in substance; the burden does not run (Austerberry; Rhone v Stephens)
Halsall v Brizell: the road deed obliges payment, but the burden must be relevant to the benefit; the hedge obligation is unrelated to road use (Thamesmead v Allotey)
Benefit to Yasmin: statutory annexation under s78 (Federated Homes) to each part; land identifiable (Crest Nicholson)
Vera retains the benefit for the land she still holds and can sue on (i); Wes remains liable on (ii) as original covenantor (and on (i) if the covenant extends to successors' acts)
Remedies: injunction for (i); possible s84 application by Xander; Alexander Devine on deliberate breach
Critique: positive covenants gap; Law Commission 2011 report 'Making Land Work' proposing land obligations; commonhold's limited take-up
Reasoned evaluation
Structure and use of authority
questions.modelAnswer:
Burden of (i). The covenant not to build more than one dwelling is negative in substance, so its burden can run in equity under Tulk v Moxhay (1848). Vera kept Willow Farm, which the covenant benefits, satisfying LCC v Allen [1914]. LPA s79 presumes the parties intended the burden to run, and the covenant was protected by a notice, so it binds Xander under LRA 2002 s29.

Burden of (ii). Maintaining a hedge requires work and expense, so the covenant is positive in substance. Its burden does not run at law (Austerberry v Oldham (1885)) or in equity (Rhone v Stephens [1994]). Xander does pay towards the road under the road deed, but under Halsall v Brizell [1957] and Thamesmead v Allotey (1998) a burden can only be attached to a benefit it is relevant to. Paying for the road relates to using the road, not to the hedge, so Xander is not liable on (ii). Wes remains contractually liable on (ii).

Benefit. The covenant was expressed to benefit Vera's adjoining land, so LPA s78 annexes the benefit to each part of it (Federated Homes v Mill Lodge [1980]). The land can be identified, which satisfies Crest Nicholson v McAllister [2004]. Yasmin therefore has the benefit of (i) for her part, even though her transfer was silent, and Vera keeps it for the land she still owns. Either of them can seek an injunction to stop the second house. If Xander applies under s84 to modify the covenant, Alexander Devine v Housing Solutions [2020] shows that a deliberate breach weighs heavily against him.

Evaluation. The result is hard to justify. The hedge benefits the neighbouring land, yet the promise to maintain it cannot be enforced against the current owner, simply because the obligation is positive. The workarounds, such as indemnity chains, rentcharges and artificial benefit-and-burden arrangements, are fragile. The Law Commission's 2011 report Making Land Work proposed a registrable "land obligation" that would let positive burdens run, but it has not been enacted, and commonhold is little used. Such reform is overdue.

questions.q: Zara and her husband Arlo jointly own their registered home. Arlo persuaded Zara to sign a charge to Bexley Bank securing his failing company's overdraft, telling her it was "only for six months". The bank sent Zara a letter suggesting she take advice, and her solicitor, who also acted for Arlo, signed a certificate saying he had explained the documents, but in fact spent five minutes with her. The company has collapsed, the bank seeks possession and wants to sell quickly at auction, and Zara wants time to sell privately. Advise Zara.
markScheme: Etridge (No 2): non-commercial surety, so the bank is put on inquiry
Zara must first establish undue influence or misrepresentation by Arlo (the 'six months' statement may be a misrepresentation)
Bank's protection depends on its steps: direct communication, solicitor confirmation; a solicitor may act for both, but must advise properly
