Bank is generally entitled to rely on the solicitor's confirmation; the inadequate advice gives a claim against the solicitor rather than defeating the bank
If the bank had not taken the steps it would have constructive notice and the charge could be set aside against Zara
Possession: s36 AJA 1970: Zara can ask for time to sell privately (Target Home Loans v Clothier; Cheltenham & Gloucester v Krausz on sale)
Sale: Cuckmere Brick duty, but timing is the lender's choice (Silven)
LPA s91 power to order sale (Palk), though Krausz limits its use to undercut a lender's possession claim
Proceeds and any surplus (s105)
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Validity of the charge. Zara was a surety for her husband's company debts, which is a non-commercial relationship, so under Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001] the bank was put on inquiry. Zara must first prove that Arlo used undue influence or misled her. His statement that the charge was "only for six months" looks like a misrepresentation about how long and how far the security would run. If so, the question is whether the bank took reasonable steps. It contacted Zara directly and obtained a solicitor's confirmation. A solicitor may act for both spouses, but must advise the wife properly and in Arlo's absence. Unless the bank knew or should have known that the advice was inadequate, it is entitled to rely on the certificate. The charge probably binds Zara, and her remedy is a negligence claim against the solicitor. If the bank missed a required step, for example by not sending the solicitor the financial information, the charge could be set aside as against her.

Possession. For a dwelling, AJA 1970 s36 lets the court adjourn or suspend possession if the sums due are likely to be paid within a reasonable period. A private sale that will clear the debt can count, provided there is firm evidence that the sale will happen soon (Target Home Loans v Clothier [1994]). Zara needs valuations and a marketing plan from an estate agent.

Sale. Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance [1971] requires the bank to take reasonable care to obtain the true market value. Under Silven Properties v RBS [2003], however, the bank can choose when to sell. A properly marketed auction does not necessarily breach its duty. Zara could ask the court to order a sale under LPA s91 (Palk [1993]). Cheltenham & Gloucester v Krausz [1997] limits that power where it is being used to keep the lender out of possession and the sale would not clear the debt. Any surplus after the debt is paid belongs to Zara and Arlo under s105.

questions.q: "The law of adverse possession in registered land now protects owners so effectively that it has lost its justification, while proprietary estoppel has become an unpredictable discretion." Critically evaluate both halves of this statement.
markScheme: Traditional justifications for limitation: quieting titles, ending stale claims, rewarding productive use, matching the register to reality
LRA 2002 Sch 6: 10 years, notification, counter-notice, para 5 conditions, two-year window: owners who respond almost always win
Retained roles: boundary cases (Zarb v Parry), lost owners/abandoned land, estoppel cases
Pye v Graham and Pye v UK: human rights compatibility; critique of the old law
Best v Chief Land Registrar: criminality does not bar claims; coherence point
Estoppel elements: assurance (Thorner; Cobbe), detriment (Gillett), unconscionability
Remedy: Jennings v Rice proportionality; Guest v Guest expectation starting point plus adjustments
Unpredictability critique vs structured discretion; certainty from Guest
Commercial/domestic divide and s116 proprietary effect
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Adverse possession has traditionally been justified because it prevents stale claims, secures titles, rewards people who use land and lines up legal title with long possession. In unregistered land the owner loses the right to recover after 12 years (Limitation Act 1980 ss15 and 17). That suited a system in which possession was the best evidence of title.

Under the LRA 2002 the register itself proves title, so the evidential reason weakens. Under Schedule 6 the squatter must apply after 10 years and the owner is notified. A counter-notice defeats the application unless a para 5 condition applies, and the owner then has two years to evict. This responds to JA Pye v Graham [2002], where a diligent company lost valuable land, although Pye v UK (2007) found the old law compatible with A1P1. The statement is right that attentive owners are now very well protected. It goes too far in saying the doctrine has lost its purpose. It still resolves boundary mistakes under para 5(4) (Zarb v Parry [2011]), brings land with absent owners back into use, and keeps the register in line with reality. Best v Chief Land Registrar [2015] shows that even criminal residential squatting can still count towards a claim.

Proprietary estoppel involves discretion, but structured discretion. Thorner v Major [2009] requires an assurance that is clear enough in context. Cobbe v Yeoman's Row [2008] excludes those who knowingly take a commercial risk. Gillett v Holt [2001] assesses detriment over the whole relationship, and unconscionability links the elements. The remedy has been the least predictable part. Jennings v Rice [2002] focused on proportionality, while Guest v Guest [2022] starts from fulfilling the expectation and then adjusts the award, for example for early receipt. The results still depend heavily on the facts, especially in farming families, and litigation is costly. That uncertainty is arguably the price of preventing unconscionable conduct where people did not observe the formalities.

Both halves of the statement contain some truth but go too far. Adverse possession now has a narrower role, not none, and estoppel's flexibility rests on principle rather than whim.

questions.q: "The Land Registration Act 2002 promised a register that mirrors the title, but Schedule 3 and the treatment of actual occupation mean that the mirror remains cracked." Discuss.
markScheme: Mirror, curtain and insurance principles explained
Aim of the 2002 Act: e-conveyancing, reduction of overriding interests (Law Com 271)
Sch 3 narrowed: para 2 qualifications (inquiry, obviousness/knowledge); para 3 limited for implied easements; transitional interests lapsed in 2013
Actual occupation remains: justification is protecting occupiers who cannot be expected to register (Boland)
Case law: Link Lending v Bustard and Chhokar v Chhokar showing flexible occupation
Cann and Scott on timing and the limits of occupation
Overreaching (Flegg) curtails the occupation crack for two-trustee sales
Rectification and indemnity: Swift 1st, forgery, the insurance principle
Equities by estoppel (s116) and their overriding potential
Evaluation: a deliberate policy trade-off; the alternative of compulsory registration of all rights is impractical
questions.modelAnswer:
The mirror principle says the register should show every right affecting the land. The curtain principle keeps trusts off the register. The insurance principle compensates anyone who suffers loss because of the register. The Law Commission's report behind the 2002 Act (Law Com No 271) aimed for a near-perfect mirror, partly to enable electronic conveyancing.

The Act did narrow the cracks. Schedule 3 is narrower than the old s70(1). Para 2 excludes occupiers who fail to disclose their rights when asked, and occupiers whose occupation was not obvious and whose interest the buyer did not know about. Para 3 protects implied legal easements only if they are known, obvious or recently used, and equitable easements no longer override. Several transitional overriding interests lapsed in 2013.

Actual occupation is the main crack that remains, and it is deliberate. People with informal beneficial interests rarely think of registering them, and Boland [1981] shows why occupation should protect them. The courts take a flexible view of occupation. Link Lending v Bustard [2010] and Chhokar v Chhokar [1984] protected occupiers who were away from home in hospital. Buyers can reduce the risk by inspecting the property and asking questions.

Other doctrines limit the crack. Overreaching (City of London BS v Flegg [1988]) protects buyers who pay two trustees. Abbey National v Cann [1991] and Scott v Southern Pacific [2014] protect lenders who fund a purchase. Under Schedules 4 and 8, the register can be corrected after a forgery and indemnity paid (Swift 1st v Chief Land Registrar [2015]), so the insurance principle supports the mirror. By contrast, s116 makes estoppel equities proprietary, and they can override through occupation, which widens the crack for informal family arrangements.

The mirror is cracked, but by design. Parliament chose to protect vulnerable occupiers at the expense of complete reliability for buyers. Requiring every informal right to be registered would be unrealistic, so a small, well-defined crack is a defensible compromise.

questions.q: Carla mortgaged her flat to Dune Finance in 2019 to secure a business loan. The mortgage deed (i) prevents redemption for 15 years, (ii) requires Carla to buy all her shop's stock from Dune's subsidiary for the life of the loan "and for five years after repayment", and (iii) gives Dune an option, granted in a separate deed signed two years later in return for a fresh loan, to buy the flat at market value. Carla now wants to redeem. Advise her.
markScheme: Equity of redemption and the rule against clogs explained

(i) Postponement: valid unless it makes the right to redeem illusory or is oppressive/unconscionable; Knightsbridge v Byrne (commercial parties); contrast Fairclough v Swan Brewery (lease), and consider whether Carla had equal bargaining power
Regulation: possible FCA/consumer protection, though it is a business loan
(ii) Collateral advantage during the loan: Kreglinger test
The post-redemption element is invalid: Noakes v Rice, Bradley v Carritt
Severability of the offending part
(iii) Option: Samuel v Jarrah Timber is void if part of the mortgage transaction
Reeve v Lisle: an option in a separate, later independent transaction can be valid; consider whether the option was truly separate
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Equity protects the right to redeem against clogs.

(i) Postponing redemption for 15 years. Postponement is not void in itself. In Knightsbridge Estates v Byrne [1939], a 40-year postponement agreed between commercial parties of equal strength was upheld. By contrast, in Fairclough v Swan Brewery [1912] a postponement that made redemption almost worthless was struck down, since the security was a lease that would have almost run out. Carla's flat is presumably freehold or held on a long lease, so redeeming after 15 years still has value. The term is likely to be valid unless Carla can show it was oppressive or unconscionable, for example because there was a large imbalance in bargaining power and the term was imposed in a morally reprehensible way. As a business loan, consumer protection probably does not apply.

(ii) The stock-buying tie. Under Kreglinger v New Patagonia Meat [1914], a collateral advantage is valid if it is not unfair or unconscionable and does not clog redemption. A tie lasting for the life of the loan is likely to be acceptable as a commercial term. The part that continues for five years after repayment is the problem. Noakes v Rice [1902] and Bradley v Carritt [1903] struck down ties that survived redemption, because the property would not be returned free of the mortgage. Kreglinger upheld a post-redemption agreement only because it was a separate contract. Here the tie appears in the mortgage deed itself, so the post-redemption part is probably void. It can be severed, leaving the rest of the mortgage intact.

(iii) The option. Samuel v Jarrah Timber [1904] makes an option to buy, granted as part of the mortgage, void. In Reeve v Lisle [1902], however, an option granted later in a genuinely separate transaction was upheld. Dune's option was granted two years later, by a separate deed, in return for new money. That suggests it is valid, unless the arrangement was in substance a single scheme.

Carla can redeem after the postponement period ends, free of the post-redemption tie. The option is probably enforceable.

questions.q: Emil worked on his uncle Felix's farm from age 16 to 46 for minimal wages, turning down a job elsewhere. Felix regularly said in front of neighbours, "This will all be Emil's one day". In 2024 Felix fell out with Emil and made a will leaving the farm to charity. Felix died in 2026, and his executors want Emil to leave the farmhouse he lives in. Advise Emil.
markScheme: Identify proprietary estoppel as the claim (no s2 contract; no will provision)
Assurance: repeated, in context, intended to be relied upon (Thorner v Major; Gillett v Holt); a will can be changed but repeated assurances may be irrevocable in effect
Reliance: turning down another job, long work
Detriment: low wages, lost opportunities; balanced against benefits such as housing (Gillett; Henry v Henry)
Unconscionability of going back
Remedy: Guest v Guest, starting with expectation (the farm), adjusted for proportionality, accelerated receipt and benefits already received
Effect against executors/estate; s116 equity binds successors; occupation
Possible alternatives: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 claim (nephew is not automatically eligible unless maintained)
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
With no s2 contract and no gift by will, Emil's claim lies in proprietary estoppel.

Assurance. Felix repeated in front of neighbours that the farm would be Emil's. In Thorner v Major [2009] less explicit statements were enough, because they were clear in their context and meant to be relied on. Promises about inheritance are not automatically revocable because wills can be changed. In Gillett v Holt [2001], repeated assurances that a claimant would inherit a farm were treated as binding once he had relied on them.

Reliance and detriment. Emil worked for 30 years on minimal wages and turned down outside work. Gillett assesses detriment broadly. The court will set off benefits Emil received, such as the farmhouse he lived in, and in Henry v Henry [2010] those benefits were weighed in the balance. Thirty years of low wages and lost career chances are still likely to outweigh what he received.

Unconscionability. Leaving the farm to charity after Emil spent his working life relying on Felix's promise is the kind of unfair conduct equity prevents.

Remedy. Under Guest v Guest [2022], the court starts by asking whether to fulfil the expectation, which here is the whole farm. It then adjusts the award so that it is not out of all proportion to the detriment. No discount for accelerated receipt is needed, because Emil receives his entitlement only on Felix's death, as promised. Benefits he has already enjoyed, such as living in the farmhouse, could however lower the award. The court might give him the farm outright, the farmhouse plus a sum of money, or a monetary award reflecting the value of his expectation.

Effect. The equity arose during Felix's lifetime and binds his estate, so the executors are subject to it. LRA 2002 s116 makes it proprietary, and Emil's occupation protects it against any buyer. He should resist possession and counterclaim. An Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975 claim is weaker: as a nephew he must show Felix was maintaining him before death.

Emil has a strong estoppel claim and is likely to receive substantial relief, quite possibly the farm itself.

questions.q: "The rule that an easement cannot amount to exclusive possession of the servient land is sound in principle but has become unworkable in practice, particularly for parking." Critically evaluate this statement in light of the case law.
markScheme: States the ouster principle and its rationale: an easement is a right over another's land, not ownership of it
Copeland v Greenhalf: extensive storage over a strip, so not an easement
Batchelor v Marlow: whether the servient owner retains reasonable use; on the facts, illusory ownership
Moncrieff v Jamieson (Lord Scott): test of retained possession and control, criticising the reasonable-use test; Lord Neuberger's caution
Later cases: Virdi v Chana and Kettel v Bloomfold upholding parking in a defined space
Regency Villas: extensive recreational rights accepted and the general approach to the 'capable of grant' requirement
Uncertainty: degree-based tests, conflicting authority, consequences for conveyancers
Law Commission (Making Land Work, 2011) recommended abolishing the reasonable-use test for future easements, so that a right fails only if it amounts to exclusive possession
Alternatives: leases or licences for exclusive spaces; drafting solutions
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The ouster principle reflects the nature of an easement: it is a right over someone else's land, not a share in owning it. If the dominant owner's use leaves the servient owner with nothing of value, the right is really a disguised transfer of possession, which should be granted as a lease or a freehold. In that sense the statement is right that the principle is sound.

Copeland v Greenhalf [1952] refused to recognise a right to store vehicles over a whole strip of land. Batchelor v Marlow [2003] went further and treated a right to park six cars during working hours as leaving the servient owner's ownership illusory. Its test was whether the owner kept reasonable use of the land. This degree-based test is hard to apply consistently.

In Moncrieff v Jamieson [2007], a Scottish appeal, Lord Scott criticised the Batchelor test. He suggested the question should be whether the servient owner keeps possession and control of the land, even if very little practical use remains. Lord Neuberger expressed sympathy but left the point open. Later English cases leaned towards Lord Scott's view. Virdi v Chana [2008] and Kettel v Bloomfold [2012] upheld rights to park in a defined space where the servient owner kept ownership and some control. Regency Villas v Diamond Resorts [2018], recognising extensive recreational rights, reflects a generally generous approach to what can be granted.

The statement is fair about the confusion. Conveyancers cannot be sure whether an exclusive parking space is an easement. If it is not, the right is a licence, which will not bind successors, unless it is drafted as a lease or a demise of the space. The Law Commission's 2011 report Making Land Work recommended abolishing the reasonable-use test for future easements, so that a right such as parking would fail only if it amounted to exclusive possession. That approach would be clearer, but it has not been enacted.

The principle is therefore sound, but the test courts use to apply it is uncertain. Adopting the Law Commission's approach would largely solve the practical problem.
